questions.q: Besides the model's parameters, what else must a checkpoint capture to resume training along the same trajectory?
options: Nothing else -- model weights alone are sufficient
The optimizer state, scheduler state, step counter, and data loader position
Only the learning rate value as a single float
The entire source code of the training script
questions.explain: A full checkpoint needs optimizer state (e.g., Adam's moment estimates), scheduler state, the current step, and the data loader position -- skipping these causes resumed training to deviate, often with a visible loss spike.

questions.q: Why does gathering every shard onto a single rank before writing a checkpoint fail to scale for large sharded models?
options: It doesn't fail to scale -- it's the recommended approach at any size
That rank must materialize the entire model and optimizer state in memory to write it, and all I/O serializes through its single disk and network connection
Single-rank writes are always faster than sharded writes
PyTorch does not allow any rank to write files to disk
questions.explain: A single-rank gather-and-write approach requires one rank to hold the full state in memory, even though sharded training never requires that, and serializes I/O through one rank's bandwidth instead of writing in parallel.

questions.q: What does torch.distributed.checkpoint (DCP) do differently from a naive single-file save?
options: It saves only the model weights and discards optimizer state entirely
Each rank writes its own local shard directly to a shared path, and loading can reshard into a different parallelism layout than the one that saved it
It requires the resuming job to use the exact same number of GPUs as the original run
It compresses the entire model into a single zip file on rank 0
questions.explain: DCP has each rank write its own shard with no cross-rank gather, and on load it redistributes shards to whatever layout the current job uses -- which can differ from the saving job's layout.

questions.q: Why does asynchronous checkpointing matter for GPU utilization during large training runs?
options: It eliminates the need to ever save a checkpoint
It copies state to host memory quickly and overlaps the actual disk write with continued training, instead of blocking GPUs while the save completes
It makes checkpoints permanently unavailable for loading
It only works when training on a single GPU
questions.explain: Asynchronous checkpointing overlaps the I/O-bound write with ongoing training compute, so GPUs aren't idle waiting for a save that can take seconds to minutes.

questions.q: What trade-off governs how frequently a long training run should checkpoint?
options: There is no trade-off -- checkpointing as often as possible is always free
Checkpointing too rarely risks losing more compute to a failure between saves, while checkpointing too often adds I/O overhead and storage cost
Checkpoint frequency only affects the final model's accuracy, not reliability
Checkpoints should only ever be taken once, at the very end of training
questions.explain: Checkpoint frequency balances compute lost to failures between saves against the I/O and storage overhead of frequent saves, typically tuned against the cluster's observed failure rate.
